en: A Direct Discourse on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
composed by the monk Shin’aku.
The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom.
Now, wisdom and folly are from the beginning not two distinct kinds; the "other shore" and "this shore" originally share a single source.

Because one perceives the existence of body and mind, it is called folly and one dwells on this shore; because one does not perceive the existence of body and mind, it is called wisdom and one reaches the other shore.
"Sūtra" is an appellation that remains unchanging through the ten thousand ages, while "mind" refers to the eight classes [of beings].
If the primordial Lord does not change, then both ordinary beings and sages may proceed by way of that primordium;
since he is the primordial source, who could abandon this and seek unexcelled bodhi elsewhere?
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
They deliver all from suffering and calamity.

Sentient beings have never not been bodhisattvas; it is only because they do not realize that both persons and phenomena are empty that they are ensnared by suffering and calamity and are thus called sentient beings.
If they were to fully comprehend this without obstruction, who would not be a bodhisattva?
"Śāriputra, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.
That he specifically calls him by name and addresses him at this point is to indicate that the emptiness realized by the superior Bodhisattvas is not that of the Lesser Vehicle.
Riding upon the emptiness of partiality is neither a blank emptiness nor a nihilistic emptiness; it is simply the emptiness that is identical with form.
Since form can be identical with emptiness, emptiness can likewise be identical with form; therefore it is said: "Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form.
Within the five aggregates, form is one; since form and emptiness can thus be mutually identical, so too can the remaining aggregates.
Because it is likewise so, it is said that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.
Śāriputra, the empty characteristic of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; and no forms.

There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; and from the absence of the realm of the eye up to the absence of the realm of consciousness.

There is no ignorance, nor is there the end of ignorance; and so on, up to there being no old age and death, nor the end of old age and death. There is no suffering, no accumulation, no cessation, and no path;
there is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained.

Calling his name once more at this point, the Buddha addresses him because he fears that his habitual tendencies toward narrow views are so deep-rooted that it will be difficult for him to suddenly enter the great ocean of the Dharma of the two-fold emptiness of Mahāyāna; therefore, he reveals the truth clearly and openly to enlighten him:
"The empty nature of all phenomena is like ice with physical obstruction which, having already melted into water, becomes square when placed in a square vessel."
When it is in a round vessel, it becomes round accordingly; when touched by wind, it can produce the sound of waves; when reflected on the ground, it can take on the color of the sky;
in rivers and lakes, it can float ten thousand bushels of grain; in great droughts, it can become clouds and rainbows. There is nowhere it does not find its own ease.
Furthermore, the analogy of round and square vessels represents the preceding objects of experience (*viṣaya*). These preceding objects of experience...
Arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease exist inherently, like water forming ice; there is nothing that is not characterized by substantial obstruction.

If a student understands this, then the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination, and the four noble truths will all become as clear as if seen before one’s eyes.
Nevertheless, objects cannot empty themselves; they must rely on illumination to be emptied. When the objects are empty, the wisdom remains; when the illness is gone, the medicine is discarded.

Existence in the end is not the fundamental substance; even medicine is a method for washing away stains. Because all defilements are thus exhausted, it is said: "There is neither ignorance nor attainment.
By relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva’s mind is free from hindrance; because there is no hindrance, [he has no fear].
There is no fear; far removed from all perverted dreams and delusions, one attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*.
All Buddhas of the three periods of time, by relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra.
This mantra is able to eliminate all suffering; because it is true and not false, I shall now speak the Prajñāpāramitā mantra.
Thus the mantra is spoken: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*.
Alas! How profound is the difficulty of transforming those whose habits are biased and narrow!
Therefore, the Tathāgata has taught this in various ways to cause them to have deep faith;
for it is not only Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva who, by relying on this Prajñāpāramitā, attains nirvāṇa with a mind free from hindrance, but all Buddhas of the three periods of time as well.
Having thereby attained unsurpassed Bodhi, I still fear that their alarm and doubt have not been fully dispelled; therefore, I issue this further decree:
"This Prajñāpāramitā is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, an unsurpassed mantra, and an unequaled mantra.
'Divine' means its majestic spiritual power is unfathomable; 'illuminating' means there is no hidden darkness it does not penetrate; it is unsurpassed."
Thus, there is nothing superior to this; being peerless, there is nothing that can equal it.
The Sage’s work for all beings is ultimate and exhaustive; nothing more can be added. It is as if one were reciting secret mantras to empower them.
When I read this sutra to this point, tears suddenly flowed down my face in profusion, which I could not restrain. This was because I was suffering from an illness at Tanzhe Temple.
While dwelling among the mountains, I recall the late Vice Minister Xu Yanwei, who was diligent in the Dharma; I have explained this to comfort and benefit his path of mind.
*The Direct Exposition of the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom* (End).
